claims.title: How many powers of ℓ divide an iterate of the parameter?
claims.hypotheses: Use a local Breuil–Kisin datum with Eisenstein polynomial E of degree e. The period ring is the ℓ-adically completed divided-power envelope and the image of E lies in its divided-power ideal.
claims.statement: For every fixed c and M the power v^(ℓⁿ−1) is divisible in the crystalline ring by ℓ^(cn+M) for all sufficiently large n.

claims.title: How do the two Frobenius evaluations compare?
claims.hypotheses: The height-H coefficient matrices satisfy AA′=E^{2H}I. Compare Frobenius evaluation of each series at the parameter with Frobenius evaluation of its constant term.
claims.statement: After division by the two unit factors the normalized matrix pairs have product ℓ^{2H}I. Multiplying their forward difference by ℓ gives entrywise divisibility by v^ℓ.

claims.title: How do the Frobenius iterates give an integral section?
claims.hypotheses: Fix the local datum and height. The growth inequality holds in the ℓ-torsion-free complete crystalline ring.
claims.statement: Two integral matrices intertwine the moving and constant Frobenius coefficients, reduce to the same power of ℓ times the identity modulo v and multiply to the square of that scalar times the identity. The exponent can be chosen uniformly in the rank.

claims.title: Why does the crystalline congruence give an exactly invariant section?
claims.hypotheses: The frame satisfies both Frobenius–Galois compatibility and the crystalline congruence. Use the two integral matrices and scalar from the Frobenius section.
claims.statement: The twisted Galois defect of the section is zero for every local Galois element.

claims.title: Which columns give the crystalline periods of the representation?
claims.hypotheses: The integral frame provides opposite period matrices whose product is τ^{2H}I. The period τ is primitive, and the chosen period datum identifies the crystalline ring with its Galois action.
claims.statement: After normalization the product of the period matrix and the section is an invertible invariant matrix over the crystalline period ring. Its columns give a basis of crystalline periods over the maximal unramified subfield.

claims.title: How do periods of a matrix lattice reach the original representation?
claims.hypotheses: The rationalized matrix lattice contains the identity and the local group acts by left multiplication. The target has a finite field of definition.
claims.statement: For each target vector there is an equivariant evaluation taking the identity to that vector. Images of the crystalline periods of the matrix lattice span all of the target after extension to the period ring.

claims.title: How can one test an algebraic trace with unramified scalars?
claims.hypotheses: Let F be an intermediate field between the ℓ-adic field and its algebraic closure. A finite set of elements and a specified element z all have norm at most one.
claims.statement: There is an F-linear functional into F taking integral values on the finite set and giving a value at z of norm at least |z| and at most one.

claims.title: Where do the three errors in a Weil trace come from?
claims.hypotheses: At one matched layer the target and auxiliary traces are represented by the stated identities for every unramified-linear functional, with one common integral scalar. The projection matches identity vectors and period operators to the given precision.
claims.statement: The weighted trace discrepancy is the exact sum of the operator and identity-vector error, the basis-trace errors, and the negative scalar-coordinate error.

claims.title: Why does agreement at arbitrarily high precision determine the trace?
claims.hypotheses: One target trace and a common integral scalar, invertible over the crystalline period ring, work for all precisions. At every precision a layer gives the required integral intertwining and both scalar estimates.
claims.statement: The realized Weil trace equals the prescribed scalar. In the application the compatible period-operator and trace realization theorems supply the hypotheses.
